Does a walk in nature change how the brain rests?

A randomized study of 92 adults finds different mood and resting EEG responses after nature and urban walks.

A busy street asks something of your attention. A green trail asks something else. I wonder what stays with the brain once the walk is over. A randomized field experiment measured mood and brain activity before and after forty minutes of walking, in nature or in the city.

The experiment

McDonnell and Strayer randomly assigned 92 adults to a 40-minute walk in a natural or urban environment (46 per group). Participants completed a mentally demanding task beforehand. Researchers measured positive and negative affect with PANAS and frontal midline theta (FMθ) using EEG. Walking duration, pace, distance, elevation, heart rate, temperature and humidity were matched or assessed.

What changed

Positive affect rose from 24.26 to 32.98 after the nature walk and from 23.07 to 28.80 after the urban walk. The time-by-environment interaction was significant (χ²(2)=9.11, p<0.05). Resting FMθ changed from 2.41 to 2.26 μV²/Hz in nature and from 2.34 to 2.99 in the urban group; the interaction was significant (χ²(3)=18.94, p<0.001). Negative affect decreased after both walks without a significant group-by-time interaction (p=0.850).

Architectural interpretation

For me, the route I walk every day is architecture. A street, the edge of a park, a green path: someone decided how they look and how they feel. Here the walk in nature went together with a larger rise in positive mood and a different resting EEG pattern than the walk in the city. But the study compared whole environments. It cannot separate the trees from traffic, noise, visual complexity or the feeling of safety. It tells me that green routes belong in the plan, and that each of their qualities deserves to be tested on its own.

Limits and conclusion

After the walk, the study measured mood and resting EEG. Neither is a direct test of cognitive performance. FMθ is an indirect neural marker, not a count of synapses or evidence of neuroplasticity. There were no measures of brain structure, gene expression, epigenetics or DNA sequence. The sample was demographically limited and long-term outcomes are unknown. A future controlled study should independently vary greenery, traffic and sound while measuring EEG, stress and objective attention.

McDonnell & Strayer (2024)
The influence of a walk in nature on human resting brain activity: a randomized controlled trial. Scientific Reports, 14, 27253.
